processing: Small unopened buds, usually described as dried in sunlight. Accounts of the golden colour differ: some credit the drying alone, and one seller describes a brief treatment with a cooled tea extract.
harvest_season: Hand-picked as unopened buds; no fixed season is well documented, and only a very small quantity is made each year.
appearance_dry: Slender, unopened buds in a pale white-gold.
appearance_liquor: Typically a pale gold, clear liquor.
appearance_wet: Soft, intact buds in a light golden olive.
taste_profile: Mellow and softly sweet with gentle florals; tasters also mention hay and pollen, with a slight drying finish.

brewing.notes: Usually brewed Western-style. Cooler water keeps delicate buds from turning flat; this follows common practice for bud white teas.

vintage_note: Sold in very small lots, often in gift tins, and usually without a harvest date. As with other bud-only white teas, freshness matters, so buy from sellers who state the year and estate.
description:
Ceylon Golden Tips is a white tea from Sri Lanka made from small, unopened buds. Think of silver needle, but with a white-gold colour instead of silver. Sri Lanka's Export Development Board notes it is usually grown at higher altitudes and that very little is made each year.

The method is reported as simple: hand-picked buds dried in sunlight. The colour is where accounts part ways. Some sellers present it as a result of drying, while one Sri Lankan retailer says the buds meet a cooled extract of conventional tea. Ask the seller, because this changes what you are drinking.

Expect a mellow, sweet, floral cup with a hay-like note. Do not expect strength. Keep the water below boiling and give the buds a few minutes.

Watch the label. 'Golden tips' is also used for tippy black tea from Ceylon, and retailers place the white version in several districts, including Nuwara Eliya, with widely differing altitude claims. Check that the tin says white tea and names an estate.
history: Little is documented about when this style first appeared or who developed it. It is sold as a rarity within Sri Lanka's specialty white tea range, and no reliable early date or maker is on record.
